title: To You, O LORD, I Lift Up My Soul
summary: The psalmist lifts his soul to God in trust, asking not to be put to shame before his enemies. He prays to be taught God's ways and paths, asks God to remember his loving devotion rather than the sins of youth, and pleads for forgiveness for the sake of God's name. Lonely, afflicted, and surrounded by those who hate him, he asks to be guarded and set free, and the psalm ends with a prayer for the redemption of all Israel.
story: Psalm 25 follows the procession of Psalm 24, where only those with clean hands and a pure heart may ascend God's hill. Here a worshiper who knows he does not meet that standard prays anyway, asking for forgiveness, instruction, and rescue. The psalm opens with the same verb Psalm 24:4 used for lifting the soul, now lifted not to an idol but to God. It weaves together the great themes of Israel's covenant: God's ways and paths, his covenant and decrees, his compassion and loving devotion, and his readiness to forgive, as he revealed himself to Moses (Exodus 34:6-7). It is the first of several psalms in Book I that turn more directly to confession of sin (compare Psalms 32 and 38).
historical:
The heading reads simply Of David. Traditional readers take the psalm as David's prayer, and some connect the sins of my youth and the enemies with his later troubles. Many modern scholars, noting that the psalm is an alphabetic acrostic, a form they associate with wisdom writing and with teaching, date it later, sometimes after the exile, and regard of David as a collection heading. The psalm names no event, and its prayer fits any faithful Israelite in trouble.

The final verse, Redeem Israel, O God, from all its distress, stands outside the alphabetic pattern and turns from the individual to the whole nation. Many scholars think it was added when the psalm was adapted for community worship, perhaps in a time of national hardship such as the exile. Others see it as the psalmist's deliberate widening of his personal prayer. Psalm 34, also an acrostic, ends with a similar extra verse, which suggests a shared convention.
cultural:
Shame in the ancient Near East was not merely an inner feeling but a public loss of standing. To be put to shame was to be seen to have trusted in something that failed, to be exposed before the community and one's enemies as foolish or abandoned. The psalmist's repeated plea that he not be put to shame (verses 2, 3, and 20) is therefore a plea that his trust in God be publicly vindicated.

The language of ways and paths reflects the way Israel thought about life as a road walked under instruction. Teachers in Israel's wisdom tradition, like the father in Proverbs, taught the young the way they should go. The word mesh or net in verse 15 comes from hunting: fowlers set nets and snares for birds, and the image is of a trap one cannot escape without help. Waiting for God, a phrase that recurs in the psalm, meant an active, expectant hope, like a watchman looking for the morning.
literary: Psalm 25 is an alphabetic acrostic: each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to tav. The pattern is not perfect. One or two letters are missing or doubled, and verse 22 falls outside the alphabet, so scholars debate whether the text suffered in copying or whether the poet worked with freedom. The acrostic form suggests completeness (the whole of one's prayer, from A to Z) and made the psalm easy to memorize. It mixes prayer and teaching: petitions addressed to God (verses 1 to 7 and 16 to 22) frame a central section that speaks about God in the third person (verses 8 to 15), describing how he guides the humble and confides in those who fear him. At the exact center, verse 11, stands the prayer for forgiveness.

outline.t: I lift up my soul: let me not be put to shame
Teach me your paths; remember your mercy, not my sins
The LORD guides the humble in his ways
For your name's sake, forgive my iniquity
The LORD confides in those who fear him
Turn to me: lonely, afflicted, and surrounded

doctrines.note: The psalmist asks God to forgive for the sake of his own name, grounding forgiveness in God's character rather than in the petitioner's worth. It is grace, not merit.
He asks God to remember not the sins of his youth but God's own loving devotion, and to take away all his sins. Repentance here is honest, specific, and full of hope.
Much of the psalm is a prayer to be taught God's ways. It shows that guidance comes to the humble and to those who fear the LORD, and that learning God's way is part of prayer, not separate from it.
God's paths are loving and faithful to those who keep his covenant and decrees, and he reveals his covenant to those who fear him. The psalm lives inside the covenant relationship.

words.note: Qavah, to wait for, to hope in. The root is related to a word for a cord, and the verb carries the sense of a tense, expectant waiting. It appears in verses 3, 5, and 21, and it describes the posture of the whole psalm: not passive resignation, but trust stretched toward God.

Salach, to forgive. In the Old Testament this verb always has God as its subject; people are never said to salach one another. It appears here at the center of the psalm, and the reason given is striking: forgive my iniquity, for it is great.

Sod, a council, a circle of confidants, or the confidential counsel shared within it. In verse 14 the LORD confides in those who fear him: he takes them into his confidence as trusted friends. The same word describes the prophets standing in the council of the LORD (Jeremiah 23:18).

Padah, to ransom or redeem, to free someone by payment or intervention. It is used of God redeeming Israel from slavery in Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8). The psalm ends by asking God to do for all Israel what he did at the exodus.

christ: Psalm 25 prays for things the New Testament says God gives in Christ: forgiveness of great iniquity for the sake of God's name, the revelation of his covenant, and redemption for Israel. God's forgiveness for his name's sake is echoed in 1 John 2:12, where believers are told their sins are forgiven on account of his name. The New Testament does not quote Psalm 25, so its link with Christ is through these shared themes rather than a direct prophecy. Its closing prayer, Redeem Israel, O God, was the hope of those like the prophetess Anna, who spoke of Jesus to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke 2:38). And Jesus, who called himself the way, is the one in whom Christians believe the prayer Show me Your ways, O LORD is finally answered.
questions: The psalmist asks God to remember his loving devotion instead of the sins of youth. What past failures do you need to hand over to God's memory in this way?
Verse 14 says the LORD confides in those who fear him. What does friendship with God look like in practice for you?
The psalm moves from my distress to Israel's distress at the end. How might your own prayers widen to include your community?
